question: Do I need a fractional CRO for my healthtech company?
body:
## Direct Answer

Most healthtech companies between roughly $2M and $30M in revenue benefit from a fractional CRO when revenue has stalled, the go-to-market motion is misfiring, or the founder is still the de facto head of sales — but you almost certainly do not need one before product-market fit or if a strong full-time VP already owns the number. A fractional CRO gives you senior revenue architecture, payer-and-provider GTM expertise, and board-ready forecasting at a fraction of a full-time executive's cost, which fits the long sales cycles and regulatory drag unique to healthtech.

The honest answer is that "do I need one" is the wrong first question. The better question is what specific revenue problem you are trying to solve, and whether that problem calls for strategic leadership versus more reps, better ops, or simply time. Healthtech adds wrinkles most fractional-CRO advice ignores: 9-to-18-month enterprise health-system sales cycles, HIPAA and procurement gatekeeping, reimbursement-dependent buyers, and a board that wants SaaS-style growth from a category that rarely behaves like SaaS. This essay walks through when a fractional CRO earns their fee in healthtech specifically, what they should own, how to structure the engagement, and how to know it worked.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do in a healthtech company?

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a part-time senior executive — typically one to three days a week — who owns the entire revenue engine: sales, marketing alignment, revenue operations, pricing, partnerships, and the forecast the board sees. Unlike a consultant who produces a deck and leaves, a fractional CRO carries a number, sits in your leadership meetings, manages your reps or sales leaders directly, and is accountable for pipeline and bookings. The "fractional" part means you rent that seniority for the fraction of the week your stage actually needs, rather than paying $300K-plus base plus equity for a full-timer you cannot yet keep busy.

In healthtech the job is materially different from selling generic B2B software. The fractional CRO has to speak the language of the buyer on the other side of the table — a health-system CIO, a VP of clinical operations, a payer's medical director, or a practice administrator — each with distinct budget cycles, security reviews, and clinical-validation demands. They build a motion that survives a procurement process where a legal and infosec review can add two quarters to a deal, and where a champion can be transferred, retire, or lose budget mid-cycle. A good one has already sold into these buyers, knows how to price around reimbursement and value-based-care contracts, and can tell your board why a healthtech pipeline converts slower than the SaaS benchmarks they keep quoting. For a deeper breakdown of the role's scope, see our guide on [what a chief revenue officer owns](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-role-scope).

![Do I need a fractional CRO for my healthtech company — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9021-b1.jpg)


The other half of the job is internal. Most sub-$20M healthtech companies have a revenue function that grew by accretion — a founder who sold the first ten logos, two or three reps hired on gut, a marketing contractor, and a CRM nobody trusts. The fractional CRO's real deliverable in the first ninety days is usually not a signed deal; it is a diagnosis of why the existing motion does not scale and a sequenced plan to fix it.

## When do you genuinely need one and when do you not?

The clearest signal you need a fractional CRO is a revenue plateau paired with founder-led sales. If you crossed $2M to $5M on the founder's relationships and network, and growth has flattened because the founder is the only person who can close, you have a repeatability problem, not a demand problem. A fractional CRO's core job is to extract what lives in the founder's head — the qualification instincts, the objection handling, the champion-building — and turn it into a documented, coachable motion other people can run. That handoff is one of the highest-leverage moments in a company's life, and it is exactly the kind of work a seasoned revenue leader has done repeatedly.

![Do I need a fractional CRO for my healthtech company — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl9021-b2.jpg)


You also need one when the board or a new raise has reset expectations and nobody in the building has scaled revenue past your current stage. Post-Series-A healthtech companies frequently hire reps and spend on marketing before anyone has designed the actual go-to-market system those reps and dollars are supposed to feed. The result is a leaky, expensive motion. A fractional CRO installs the architecture — ICP definition, segmentation, pricing, sales stages, forecast discipline — before you pour more fuel in. Our breakdown of [go-to-market motions for regulated industries](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/gtm-regulated-industries) covers why healthtech in particular punishes companies that scale headcount ahead of process.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Revenue has stalled] --> B{Is founder still the main closer}
    B -->|Yes| C[Repeatability gap]
    B -->|No| D{Do you have a strong revenue leader}
    D -->|Yes| E[Coach or advise not hire]
    D -->|No| F[Leadership gap]
    C --> G[Fractional CRO fits]
    F --> G
    A --> H{Do you have product market fit}
    H -->|No| I[Fix product first not sales]
    H -->|Yes| B

![Do I need a fractional CRO for my healthtech company — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9021-b3.jpg)

```

Now the cases where you do not need one. If you have not reached product-market fit, a fractional CRO cannot save you — a great revenue leader selling a product the market does not want just burns your runway faster and more convincingly. Fix the product and the value proposition first. Second, if you already employ a capable full-time VP of Sales or CRO who owns the number and is hitting it, adding a fractional executive above them creates confusion, not leverage; what that leader may need instead is a focused advisor or a coach, not a second boss. Third, if your entire problem is execution volume — you have a proven motion and just need more reps running it — hire reps and a manager, not a strategist. Paying CRO-level rates for work a sales manager can do is a waste. And fourth, if you are pre-revenue and pre-team, there is nothing yet to lead; you need a founder who can sell, not an executive to manage a team of zero.

## How is healthtech different from generic SaaS for revenue leadership?

Three structural facts make healthtech revenue harder, and they are the reason a generalist fractional CRO can fail even when they are individually excellent. First is the sales cycle. Enterprise health-system deals routinely run nine to eighteen months from first meeting to signature because they pass through clinical validation, infosec and HIPAA review, procurement, and often a committee that includes people who will never use your product. A CRO whose entire career was 30-to-90-day SaaS cycles will forecast wrong, staff wrong, and burn out reps who expected faster wins. You want someone who has lived inside these cycles and knows how to keep a deal warm across two budget years.

Second is the buyer-payer split. In much of healthtech, the person who buys is not the person who pays and not the person who uses. A digital-health tool might be championed by a clinician, budgeted by an administrator, reimbursed by a payer, and used by a patient. Pricing and packaging have to account for reimbursement codes, value-based-care contracts, and the reality that ROI has to be provable in clinical or financial terms the buyer can defend internally. A fractional CRO who understands this can build a motion around it; one who does not will keep pitching features to people who care about outcomes and defensibility.

Third is regulatory and trust friction. Every deal carries a security review, a BAA, and often a clinical-evidence bar. This is not overhead to route around — it is part of the sale, and the best healthtech revenue leaders build it into the motion so that infosec and compliance become accelerants rather than surprises that stall the deal in the final quarter. If you are weighing this against building the capability internally, our comparison of [fractional versus full-time revenue leadership](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-vs-fulltime-revenue) lays out the tradeoffs by stage.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[First meeting] --> B[Clinical validation]
    B --> C[Security and HIPAA review]
    C --> D[Procurement and legal]
    D --> E[Budget approval]
    E --> F[Signature]
    F --> G[Implementation and go live]
    G --> H[Expansion and renewal]
```

The diagram above is not decoration — it is the map a healthtech CRO has to manage against. Each stage has a different owner, a different objection, and a different way to die. A revenue leader who cannot name the champion, the blocker, and the economic buyer at every one of those stages is not running your pipeline; they are hoping.

## What should a fractional CRO own in the first 90 days?

Structure the engagement around outcomes, not hours. In the first thirty days a strong fractional CRO diagnoses: they audit your pipeline, listen to call recordings, interview your reps and your last five won and lost deals, and pressure-test your ICP against who actually buys and renews. The deliverable is a written revenue diagnosis — where deals stall, which segments convert, what your true sales cycle and win rate are, and where the motion breaks. In healthtech this almost always surfaces a mismatch between who you think you sell to and who actually signs.

In days thirty to sixty they design and begin installing the system: a defined ICP and segmentation, a stage-gated sales process mapped to the real buying journey above, a forecast methodology the board can trust, pricing and packaging aligned to how healthtech buyers actually budget, and the revenue-operations plumbing to measure all of it. By days sixty to ninety they should be operating — running the forecast call, coaching reps live, personally advancing a few strategic deals to prove the motion, and giving you a clear read on whether your team has the right people in the right seats. A frequent and uncomfortable output of month three is a personnel recommendation: the rep who was great at founder-fed inbound may not survive a real outbound motion.

Tie compensation to this arc. Fractional CRO engagements commonly blend a monthly retainer with equity and sometimes a performance component tied to pipeline or bookings, but do not over-index on short-term bookings in a business with an 18-month cycle — you will incentivize the wrong behavior. Reward leading indicators the CRO can actually influence inside the engagement window: qualified pipeline created, forecast accuracy, motion documentation, and key hires made. Set a defined review point, usually at ninety days and again at six months, where you jointly decide to continue, convert the role to full-time, or wind it down because the system is now self-running.

## How much does a fractional CRO cost, and how do you measure ROI?

Fractional CRO pricing varies widely by seniority, time commitment, and equity mix, so avoid anchoring on a single number — get quotes and compare structure, not just headline rate. The consistent pattern is that you pay materially less than a full-time CRO's total compensation because you are buying a fraction of the week and rarely the full equity grant a full-timer commands. The real cost question is not the retainer; it is opportunity cost. A cheap fractional CRO who does not know healthtech buyers can waste two quarters of runway learning your market on your dime, which is far more expensive than a higher rate paid to someone who already sold into health systems.

Measure ROI against the diagnosis they wrote in month one, not against a vanity bookings number. Did forecast accuracy improve? Did qualified pipeline grow and did the composition of that pipeline shift toward your real ICP? Did the founder get pulled out of every deal? Did you make one or two hires that would have taken you six months and a mis-hire to figure out alone? In a long-cycle business, the honest measure of a good fractional CRO at ninety days is a healthier, more predictable pipeline and a motion your team can run without them — the closed revenue often lands after the engagement, which is exactly why you tie comp to leading indicators. For benchmarking your own funnel against these signals, our [revenue operations metrics reference](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-metrics-benchmarks) is a useful companion.

The strongest fractional engagements are designed to make themselves unnecessary. The best-case ending is that the system is documented, the forecast is trustworthy, the right full-time leader is in the seat, and the fractional CRO's days-per-week can taper. If a fractional CRO seems to be engineering permanent dependency rather than building capability, that is a signal to reassess — you are paying for a system and a handoff, not an indefinite outsourced executive.

## Related questions

### How is a fractional CRO different from a sales consultant?
A consultant advises and hands you a plan; a fractional CRO carries the number, manages your team directly, sits in leadership meetings, and is accountable for pipeline and forecast outcomes — execution, not just recommendations.

### Can a fractional CRO help before product-market fit?
Generally no. Without PMF, better revenue leadership just spends runway faster. Fix the product and value proposition first; a fractional CRO is for scaling a motion that already shows signs of working.

### Should a healthtech startup hire a fractional CRO or a VP of Sales?
A VP of Sales executes an existing motion; a fractional CRO designs the motion and the broader revenue system. If you lack the system, start fractional-CRO; if you have the system and need volume, hire a VP.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run six to twelve months with a ninety-day checkpoint. The goal is to install a self-running system and either taper the role or convert it to full-time once revenue justifies the cost.

### Does industry experience really matter for a healthtech CRO?
Yes, more than in most sectors. Long cycles, payer-provider buyer splits, HIPAA and procurement friction, and reimbursement-driven pricing mean a generalist can burn quarters learning what a healthtech-native leader already knows.

## FAQ

**Is a fractional CRO worth it for a company under $2M in revenue?**
Usually not. Below $2M you typically need founder-led selling and product iteration, not senior revenue architecture. The exception is a founder who genuinely cannot or should not sell and has capital to invest in building the motion early.

**Can one fractional CRO work across multiple companies at once?**
Yes, and most do — that portfolio model is how the economics work. Ask about their current load; a CRO stretched across five clients may not give your healthtech deals the attention long cycles demand.

**Will a fractional CRO manage my existing sales reps directly?**
A true fractional CRO does, including running the forecast call and coaching live. If a candidate only wants to advise from the sidelines, you are hiring a consultant, and you should price and expect accordingly.

**How quickly will we see results from a fractional CRO?**
Expect a diagnosis in thirty days and an installed system by ninety, but in healthtech closed revenue often lands after the engagement window because of the sales cycle. Measure early results by pipeline health and forecast accuracy, not bookings.

**What happens when the fractional CRO engagement ends?**
Ideally you have a documented motion, a trustworthy forecast, and either a full-time leader in the seat or a team that can run without them. A good engagement is designed to make itself unnecessary rather than create permanent dependency.

**Do fractional CROs take equity instead of cash?**
Most engagements blend a monthly retainer with some equity, and occasionally a performance component. Be cautious tying too much comp to short-term bookings in a long-cycle business — it incentivizes the wrong behavior.

**Can a fractional CRO help us raise our next round?**
Indirectly, yes. A credible forecast, a defined ICP, and a repeatable motion are exactly what investors underwrite in healthtech. A fractional CRO who builds board-ready revenue reporting strengthens your raise even if they never talk to an investor.

**How do I vet a fractional CRO's healthtech experience?**
Ask for specific deals they closed into health systems, payers, or providers; how they handled a stalled procurement or security review; and how they priced around reimbursement. Vague answers about "enterprise SaaS" are a red flag for this category.
